description: Particle arrangements, changes of state, heating curves, and limitations of the particle model.
content_html:
The Particle Model

All matter is made of tiny particles that are too small to see. The particle model describes the three states of matter in terms of how particles are arranged, how they move, and how strongly they are held together by attractive forces.

In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement. Strong forces of attraction hold them in fixed positions. Particles cannot move from place to place — they only vibrate about their fixed positions. This gives solids a definite shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid, particles are still close together but in an irregular arrangement. The forces of attraction are weaker, allowing particles to slide past each other. Liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape — they flow to fill the bottom of a container. In a gas, particles are far apart, in no fixed arrangement. The forces of attraction are very weak, so particles move rapidly in random directions. Gases have no fixed shape or volume and expand to fill any container.

Key Fact

Solid: regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions, close together, strong forces. Liquid: irregular, slide past each other, close together, weaker forces. Gas: random, fast movement in all directions, far apart, very weak forces.

Changes of State

When matter is heated or cooled, it can change from one state to another. These are called changes of state. During a change of state, the particles themselves do not change — only their arrangement, spacing and movement change. Changes of state are physical changes: they are reversible and no new substances are produced.

Melting (solid → liquid): particles gain energy, vibrate more vigorously and overcome the forces holding them in fixed positions, so they can flow past each other. Boiling or evaporation (liquid → gas): particles gain enough energy to escape the remaining attractive forces and move freely. Condensing (gas → liquid): particles lose energy, slow down, and forces of attraction pull them closer. Freezing (liquid → solid): particles lose more energy and lock into fixed positions. Sublimation (solid → gas directly, without passing through the liquid state). Deposition (gas → solid directly).

During melting and boiling, energy is absorbed from the surroundings to break forces between particles. During condensing and freezing, energy is released to the surroundings as new forces form. Crucially, the temperature stays constant during a change of state — all the energy input goes into breaking or forming intermolecular forces rather than increasing particle kinetic energy.

Key Fact

During a change of state, temperature remains constant because energy is used to break (or form) forces between particles rather than raising kinetic energy. Changes of state are physical — reversible, no new substances formed.

Heating and Cooling Curves

A heating curve is a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated steadily. It shows a rising section (solid warming up), a flat section at the melting point (solid converting to liquid at constant temperature), another rising section (liquid warming up), and a flat section at the boiling point (liquid converting to gas at constant temperature). A cooling curve is the reverse: it shows the same flat sections at boiling point (condensation) and melting point (freezing).

A pure substance shows sharp, flat plateaux at precise melting and boiling points. An impure substance (a mixture) melts and boils over a range of temperatures rather than at a single fixed point. This is why melting point measurement is used to test the purity of a compound — a pure substance has a sharp, narrow melting range.

Physical and Chemical Changes

A physical change does not produce any new substances. The particles themselves stay the same — only their arrangement or energy changes. Physical changes are reversible under normal conditions. A chemical change forms new substances with different properties. Atoms are rearranged into new combinations; old bonds are broken and new ones form. Chemical changes are usually irreversible — for example, burning magnesium in air produces magnesium oxide, which cannot easily be turned back into magnesium and oxygen under normal conditions.

The simple particle model represents all particles as identical, inelastic, solid spheres (like tiny billiard balls). This is useful for explaining states of matter and changes of state at a basic level, but it has important limitations:

• The model does not account for the forces of attraction between particles — these are what actually hold matter together, yet the simple model treats particles as though they repel or are neutral.
• It treats all particles as having the same size and mass, when in reality different atoms and molecules have different sizes and masses.
• It does not accurately represent the actual spacing between particles in gases — particles in a gas are very much further apart than diagrams typically show.
• The model cannot explain why different substances have different melting and boiling points, because it treats all particles as identical spheres. To explain differences in properties, we need to consider the nature of the particles themselves (atoms, ions, molecules) and the bonds or intermolecular forces between them.

Key Fact

Limitations of the particle model: it treats all particles as identical spheres; it ignores forces of attraction between particles; it does not account for different particle sizes; it cannot explain why different substances have different melting and boiling points.
exam_tip_html: For ‘2 marks — Describe’ questions on particle arrangements, include both the spacing AND the movement of particles for full marks — naming one without the other usually earns only one mark. For heating curve questions, the most common error is failing to explain that temperature remains constant during a change of state. Always state the reason: energy is used to break intermolecular forces rather than raise kinetic energy. For questions distinguishing physical from chemical changes, the key test is whether new substances are formed. For Higher tier limitation questions, name a specific limitation and link it to what the simple model fails to explain.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Solids have particles in a regular, fixed arrangement that vibrate. Liquids have particles that can flow past each other. Gases have widely spaced particles moving rapidly in random directions. State determines shape and volume behaviour.
  • Changes of state are physical changes — reversible, no new substances formed. During a change of state, temperature stays constant as energy breaks or forms forces between particles. Heating curves show flat sections at melting and boiling points.
  • Physical changes do not form new substances; chemical changes do and are usually irreversible. The simple particle model has limitations: it ignores forces between particles, treats all particles as identical spheres, and cannot explain why different substances have different melting and boiling points (Higher tier).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid?
A) Regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions
B) Irregular arrangement, move randomly at high speed, far apart
C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other
D) Regular arrangement, far apart, strong attractive forces
practice_questions.marks: C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the change of state when a substance converts directly from a solid to a gas.
Describe how the temperature changes when a pure substance is heated from solid to gas, and explain what happens at the melting point.
practice_questions.marks: Temperature rises as the solid heats up, stays constant (flat section) at the melting point as the solid converts to liquid, then rises again as the liquid heats up [1 mark]; at the melting point, energy supplied is used to break forces between particles rather than raising the kinetic energy of particles, so temperature stays constant [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: A physical change does not produce any new substances and is reversible [1 mark]; a chemical change produces one or more new substances with different properties and is usually irreversible [1 mark]; example of physical: melting ice, dissolving salt (accept any valid physical change); example of chemical: burning wood, cooking food, rusting iron [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student heats a sample of an impure solid and measures its temperature over time. She notices that the substance begins to melt at 45°C and finishes melting at 52°C.
A pure sample of the same substance melts at exactly 48°C.
Explain these observations using your knowledge of the particle model.
practice_questions.marks:
A pure substance has particles of one type, all held together by forces of the same strength, so all particles overcome these forces at the same temperature, giving a sharp melting point [1 mark]
Impurities disrupt the regular arrangement of particles in the solid [1 mark]; different impurity particles are held by forces of different strengths [1 mark]; so different particles overcome these forces at different temperatures, giving a range of melting temperatures rather than a single sharp point [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two limitations of the simple particle model in describing the behaviour of matter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two limitations clearly stated with precise explanation of what each prevents the model from explaining; examples given; accurate scientific language throughout.
Secure: Two limitations described with partial explanation; some scientific terminology.
Developing: One clear limitation or two vague ones; limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement about the model without specific limitations.

Limitations may include:
(1) The model treats all particles as identical solid spheres of the same size, ignoring that different atoms, molecules and ions have different sizes and masses. This means the model cannot explain why different substances have different properties such as different melting and boiling points.
(2) The model does not represent the forces of attraction between particles. In reality it is these forces (bonds and intermolecular forces) that hold matter together and determine state. The model appears to show particles simply touching or repelling.
(3) In gas diagrams, particles are usually shown much closer together than they actually are — gas particles are typically very much further apart than solid or liquid particles.
[Award up to 3 marks per limitation: 1 for naming it, 2 for explaining what it fails to account for, 3 for linking it to a property the model cannot explain]

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state?
Which change of state is the reverse of condensation?
In a solid, particles are held in a regular arrangement and can only _____ about their fixed positions.
A _____ change produces new substances and is usually irreversible, while a physical change does not produce new substances.
Match each change of state to the correct description:

flashcard_questions.q: Describe particle arrangement in a solid.
flashcard_questions.a: Regular arrangement, close together, vibrate in fixed positions, strong forces between particles.

flashcard_questions.q: Describe particle arrangement in a gas.
flashcard_questions.a: Far apart, random arrangement, move rapidly in all directions, very weak forces between particles.
The change of state directly from solid to gas, without passing through the liquid state.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does temperature stay constant during a change of state?
flashcard_questions.a: Energy is used to break or form forces between particles, not to increase kinetic energy.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a flat section on a heating curve represent?
flashcard_questions.a: A change of state occurring at constant temperature (melting or boiling).

flashcard_questions.q: How does the melting point of an impure substance differ from that of a pure substance?
flashcard_questions.a: Impure substances melt over a temperature range, not at a single sharp point.
A change that does not create new substances and is reversible — e.g. melting or dissolving.
A change that creates new substances, usually irreversible — e.g. burning or rusting.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one limitation of the simple particle model. (Higher Tier)
flashcard_questions.a: It treats all particles as identical solid spheres and ignores forces of attraction between them.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can the simple particle model not explain different melting points? (Higher Tier)
flashcard_questions.a: It treats all particles as identical, ignoring differences in particle size, mass and intermolecular forces.

glossary_terms.definition: A scientific model that explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of the arrangement, movement and energy of particles.
The three forms in which matter can exist — solid, liquid and gas — each with different particle arrangements and properties.
A physical change in which a substance transitions between solid, liquid and gas without any new substances being formed.
A graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated at a constant rate, showing flat sections where changes of state occur at constant temperature.
A change that alters how particles are arranged or how they move, but creates no new substances and is reversible.
A change in which one or more new substances are formed, bonds between atoms are broken and reformed, and the process is usually irreversible.
